newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Fed rate inaction seen casting pall on Asia bonds.
newsitem.headline: Fed rate inaction seen casting pall on Asia bonds.

text.p: The drop in the dollar after the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady could cast a pall over bond issues by Asian borrowers, analysts said on Wednesday.
But they added that some bond issuers may still try to take advantage of low interest rates while they can.
"It's both good and bad. The outlook for rates remains subdued, but obviously the weaker dollar does not help," a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank in Hong Kong said.
The U.S. central bank opted to hold interest rates steady at its policy-making meeting on Tuesday.
The decision left the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans at 5.50 percent and the official discount rate at 5.0 percent.
U.S. stocks rallied but the dollar took the news hard, dropping a full yen to 112.65 by the end of U.S. trading. The greenback also was off two pfennigs at 1.6770 marks.

The Treasury market reacted listlessly, with short rates falling and the long end up modestly. Treasuries remained subdued in Asian trade, with the 30-year bond yielding 6.90 percent in Tokyo at midday, unchanged from the New York close.
The dollar recovered some ground during Asian trade but still remained well below levels registered earlier this week.
Analysts said the weaker dollar would dampen demand for dollar-denominated investments.

"The strength of the yen against the U.S. dollar causes some problems for Japanese investors, which are particularly big in Asian bond markets, because for them the valuations have changed," said BA Asia's research manager in Hong Kong, Raja V.
"Now a dollar investment looks like a money loser and that comes at a pretty bad time for Asia when countries like Thailand and Korea require a lot of investment through bonds," he said.
The dollar already had been under pressure, sliding some 12 percent versus the yen in the past three weeks in anticipation of an official rate increase in Japan.
"Fundamentals would still suggest that over the longer term the dollar should maintain strength in the international market against the yen and the mark," the U.S. syndicate manager said.
"But given the near-term outlook for Japanese rates rising and U.S. rates staying relatively subdued we are left with the result that we now have in the currency market," he said.
U.S. economists had been split on whether the Fed would raise rates at Tuesday's meeting, but many have forecast a tightening before the end of the year.
With that in mind, some Asian issuers may opt to raise fixed-rate funds soon rather than risk the possibility of higher rates later. The Fed policy group meets again on July 1 and 2.

"There is a general interest among issuers in locking up fixed interest rates at this stage in anticipation of rates going higher," said Paul Smith, executive director of debt capital markets at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Bankers said a number of Asian issuers are eyeing the fixed-rate Euro and Yankee bond markets.
"Issuers have an appetite to borrow and investors have an appetite to invest. But there could be a pause," said the U.S. syndicate manager.
Bankers pointed out that Asian issuance has slowed recently in the wake of financial difficulties in South Korea and Thailand and ahead of elections in Indonesia.
Volatility in the U.S. Treasury market also has dissuaded some Asian borrowers, most notably the Philippines, from tapping the U.S. Yankee market.
The Philippine central bank still plans to issue a long-dated bond, but launch is not expected soon, market sources said.
